claims.claim: Modernity has traditionally been presented as the age when artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment through a process of de-naturalization, but Hannah Arendt questioned this conviction.
Arendt's political ontology in The Human Condition is based on a phenomenological approach rooted in German Existenz-philosophy.
The search for an extraterrestrial Archimedean point involves a radical modification of the human condition.
Labor is described as a mere animal activity in Arendt's ontology, wherein humanity is considered the most dangerous of animal races.
Action is identified as the highest and most specifically human activity, taking place in the world of things created by homo faber.
Process is the antithesis of action, functioning as a sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law that creates a terrain of necessity.
Modernity in its first phase is characterized by the victory of homo faber using means-end rationality to produce artificial things, with fabrication inherently entailing violence against nature.
Fabrication inevitably involves an over-all reification of nature and acts as a destroyer of nature through an element of violation and violence.
In the second phase of modernity, animal laborans rises to dominance and technological productivity paradoxically annihilates the lasting artificial world by flooding it with natural processes.

Arendt asserts that the rationality required for constructing machines and launching artificial processes is an animal rather than a human ability, functioning as a modified animal instinct to maintain biological existence.
Modern technology does not build a lasting artificial human world, but instead serves to fulfill consumption needs and ensure the continuous functioning of human metabolism with nature.

In her closing chapter, Arendt returns to the narrative of cultural criticism where re-naturalization and the fading out of action embody the main threat of modernity rather than environmental pollution.
